lessons.title: CI/CD Mental Model and Pipeline Architecture
lessons.summary: CI/CD Mental Model and Pipeline Architecture Continuous Integration answers: can this change safely join the main branch? Continuous Delivery answers: do we have a verified artifact that could be deployed? Continuous Deployment goes one step further and actually promotes it automatically. TaskFlow separates these responsibilities…
lessons.body:
CI/CD Mental Model and Pipeline Architecture
Continuous Integration answers: can this change safely join the main branch? Continuous Delivery answers: do we have
a verified artifact that could be deployed? Continuous Deployment goes one step further and actually promotes it
automatically. TaskFlow separates these responsibilities instead of hiding them in one giant workflow.

Immutable               Environment
Commit SHA        →      Verified source    →           image          →       promotion

Build once, promote many

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Source commit is the identity of a release

• Build once; promote the same artifact

• Failures stop at the earliest honest boundary

• Production deployment is Phase 34

CI/CD terminology here is an engineering model used by TaskFlow; deployment implementation intentionally remains Phase 34.

lessons.body:
Workflow Triggers, Permissions, and
Concurrency
Use pull_request for untrusted PR verification and push/main for trusted release work. Give GITHUB_TOKEN the
minimum permissions required. Concurrency should cancel stale CI runs, but production release/deployment groups
normally should not cancel an in-progress release.

Untrusted PR     →      Read-only CI      →      Trusted main      →       Release job

Trust boundary

What this changes in TaskFlow
• CI: contents: read

• Registry publish: packages: write

• Cloud OIDC: id-token: write only where needed

• Avoid unsafe pull_request_target checkout patterns

Workflow baseline
permissions:
contents: read

concurrency:
group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
cancel-in-progress: true

GitHub recommends least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions and warns about untrusted workflow execution contexts.

lessons.summary: Node, pnpm, Monorepo Cache, and Deterministic Install CI reproduces the repository using the committed lockfile. pnpm install --frozen-lockfile should fail if package manifests and the lockfile disagree. Setup-node can cache pnpm package downloads, but the lockfile remains the dependency truth. Cache speeds installation; it must…
lessons.body:
Node, pnpm, Monorepo Cache, and Deterministic
Install
CI reproduces the repository using the committed lockfile. pnpm install --frozen-lockfile should fail if package manifests
and the lockfile disagree. Setup-node can cache pnpm package downloads, but the lockfile remains the dependency
truth. Cache speeds installation; it must never replace correctness.

Same
Lockfile        →        pnpm cache        →        Frozen install   →        dependency
graph

Deterministic install

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Node 24.21.0 course lock

• pnpm 12.3.4 course lock

• pnpm-lock.yaml committed

• Cache dependency path points at the lockfile

Deterministic setup
uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
with:
version: 12.3.4

uses: actions/setup-node@v7
with:
node-version: 24.21.0
cache: pnpm

run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

actions/setup-node v7 can cache pnpm dependencies; the committed lockfile remains the reproducibility anchor.

lessons.title: Quality Gates Lint Typecheck Test and Build
lessons.summary: Quality Gates: Lint, Typecheck, Test, and Build A pull request should fail before merge when static analysis, typechecking, tests, or a production build fails. These checks answer different questions, so a green lint step does not replace TypeScript compilation or application tests. Lint → Typecheck…
lessons.body:
Quality Gates: Lint, Typecheck, Test, and Build
A pull request should fail before merge when static analysis, typechecking, tests, or a production build fails. These checks
answer different questions, so a green lint step does not replace TypeScript compilation or application tests.

Lint         →       Typecheck        →           Tests   →     Build

Independent quality gates

What this changes in TaskFlow
• lint -> code-quality conventions

• typecheck -> compile-time correctness

• test -> behavior

• build -> deployable source graph

Required checks become useful when branch protection requires them before merge.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL Service Containers and Prisma Migrations in CI
lessons.summary: PostgreSQL Service Containers and Prisma Migrations in CI Repository and HTTP integration tests need a real PostgreSQL database. GitHub Actions service containers provide an isolated test database on Linux runners. Apply committed Prisma migrations with migrate deploy before integration tests so CI catches migration drift…
lessons.body:
PostgreSQL Service Containers and Prisma
Migrations in CI
Repository and HTTP integration tests need a real PostgreSQL database. GitHub Actions service containers provide an
isolated test database on Linux runners. Apply committed Prisma migrations with migrate deploy before integration tests
so CI catches migration drift instead of silently creating schema from models.

Repository
Postgres 18      →        Migrations         →          tests        →        HTTP E2E

Integration path

What this changes in TaskFlow
• postgres:18 service container

• health check before tests

• prisma generate

• prisma migrate deploy

• integration + HTTP E2E

Integration database
services:
postgres:
image: postgres:18
options: --health-cmd="pg_isready ..."

run: pnpm --filter api exec prisma migrate deploy

GitHub documents PostgreSQL service containers on Ubuntu/Linux runners; Prisma migrate deploy applies committed migrations.

lessons.title: Test Matrices Artifacts and Failure Diagnostics
lessons.summary: Test Matrices, Artifacts, and Failure Diagnostics Artifacts should help diagnose failed or expensive jobs, not become an uncontrolled data dump. Upload browser traces, coverage, release manifests, or test reports with explicit retention. Matrix jobs are useful when the same contract genuinely needs multiple environments; do…
lessons.body:
Test Matrices, Artifacts, and Failure Diagnostics
Artifacts should help diagnose failed or expensive jobs, not become an uncontrolled data dump. Upload browser traces,
coverage, release manifests, or test reports with explicit retention. Matrix jobs are useful when the same contract
genuinely needs multiple environments; do not multiply cost without a compatibility requirement.

Engineer
Job fails        →        Collect report      →       Upload artifact   →   inspects

Evidence on failure

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Upload useful diagnostics

• Set retention deliberately

• Do not upload secrets or .env files

• Use matrices for real compatibility coverage

actions/upload-artifact current v7 line stores diagnostic/release files; never upload secrets.

lessons.summary: Docker Buildx, Cache, and Immutable Image Tags Phase 32 created reproducible images. Phase 33 builds them in CI using Buildx and GitHub Actions cache. Every release image receives an immutable tag tied to the full Git commit SHA. Mutable labels such as main can exist…
lessons.body:
Docker Buildx, Cache, and Immutable Image Tags
Phase 32 created reproducible images. Phase 33 builds them in CI using Buildx and GitHub Actions cache. Every release
image receives an immutable tag tied to the full Git commit SHA. Mutable labels such as main can exist for convenience,
but deployments should record and promote the immutable SHA-tagged artifact.

sha-tagged
github.sha        →           Buildx          →             image      →   GHCR

Immutable image identity

What this changes in TaskFlow
• web image + api image

• Buildx gha cache

• sha- tag

• Do not rebuild during deployment

Release identity
tags:
type=sha,format=long,prefix=sha-

# deployment candidate
ghcr.io/<owner>/taskflow-api:sha-${{ github.sha }}

Current Docker action lines verified: setup-buildx v4, metadata v6, build-push v7.

lessons.summary: GHCR, GITHUB_TOKEN, and Release Manifests GitHub Container Registry can be authenticated with the workflow-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN. Only the image-publishing job needs packages: write. A release manifest records the commit and exact image reference so Phase 34 can deploy a known candidate rather than guessing which mutable…
lessons.body:
GHCR, GITHUB_TOKEN, and Release Manifests
GitHub Container Registry can be authenticated with the workflow-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN. Only the image-publishing
job needs packages: write. A release manifest records the commit and exact image reference so Phase 34 can deploy a
known candidate rather than guessing which mutable tag is current.

release
contents:read     →     packages:write     →          GHCR   →   manifest

Registry permissions

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Least privilege per workflow/job

• GHCR image namespace

• Commit SHA -> image tag

• Artifact manifest -> deployment input

GHCR workflows can publish with GITHUB_TOKEN when packages: write is granted.

lessons.body:
Secrets, OIDC, and Protected Environments
Long-lived cloud keys in repository secrets are avoidable on providers that support GitHub OIDC. The deployment job
requests a short-lived identity token with id-token: write and exchanges it with the cloud provider. Production
environments can require approval and delay access to environment secrets until protection rules pass.

Cloud trust                Short-lived
GitHub OIDC        →          policy          →          token          →           Deploy

Short-lived deployment trust

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Prefer OIDC to static cloud keys

• Environment secrets are deployment-scoped

• Approval before secret access

• Separate staging and production trust

Deployment job trust
permissions:
contents: read
id-token: write

jobs:
deploy:
environment: production

GitHub environments can gate jobs and delay environment-secret access; OIDC uses id-token: write for short-lived cloud auth.

Dependabot

Dependabot

Production hardening rule
uses: actions/checkout@<full-verified-commit-sha> # v7.x

Branch Protection, Release Gates, and
Rollback-Friendly Design
CI becomes meaningful when protected branches require its checks before merge. Release and deployment pipelines
should serialize production changes and preserve old immutable images. Rollback then means selecting the previously
known-good image, not trying to reconstruct yesterday’s source and dependencies.

Select previous                Redeploy

Rollback model

What this changes in TaskFlow
• Require CI status checks

• Do not overlap production deployments

• Keep deployment history

• Rollback by immutable artifact reference

GitHub concurrency can serialize release/deployment work; environments can add review/protection rules.

Purpose

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 33: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

Purpose
Build a trustworthy GitHub Actions pipeline that verifies pull requests, creates immutable release artifacts, uses least privilege, caches safely, and controls deployment concurrency.

Deliverable
.github/workflows/ci.yml plus release/deploy workflows that build once, tag by commit SHA, and gate promotion.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
pull request -> deterministic install -> lint/typecheck/test/build -> trusted main -> immutable artifact -> environment gate -> deployment

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Create CI triggered by pull_request with read-only contents permission and explicit concurrency cancellation.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Set up Node and pnpm, then install with --frozen-lockfile so manifests cannot drift from the lockfile.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Run lint/typecheck/tests/build as separate clear steps or jobs with understandable failure ownership.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Add dependency/package cache only after correctness works; key it from lockfile inputs.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Create trusted-main release workflow that tags an image/artifact with the commit SHA rather than latest only.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Add environment protection/permissions for deployment and ensure stale production runs are not silently canceled mid-release.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 33: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
pull request -> deterministic install -> lint/typecheck/test/build -> trusted main -> immutable artifact -> environment gate -> deployment

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Using pull_request_target with untrusted checkout/secrets
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Broad write permissions for all jobs
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Rebuilding different artifacts in each environment
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — CI green because important workspace checks never ran
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — CI/CD with GitHub Actions

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 33 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build a trustworthy GitHub Actions pipeline that verifies pull requests, creates immutable release artifacts, uses least privilege, caches safely, and controls deployment concurrency.

Required artifact
.github/workflows/ci.yml plus release/deploy workflows that build once, tag by commit SHA, and gate promotion.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can read/write a GitHub Actions workflow.
• Can explain trigger trust boundaries.
• Can enforce deterministic install.
• Can build once/promote same artifact.

Independent build sequence
1. Create CI triggered by pull_request with read-only contents permission and explicit concurrency cancellation.
2. Set up Node and pnpm, then install with --frozen-lockfile so manifests cannot drift from the lockfile.
3. Run lint/typecheck/tests/build as separate clear steps or jobs with understandable failure ownership.
4. Add dependency/package cache only after correctness works; key it from lockfile inputs.
5. Create trusted-main release workflow that tags an image/artifact with the commit SHA rather than latest only.
6. Add environment protection/permissions for deployment and ensure stale production runs are not silently canceled mid-release.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

objectives: Explain Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence.
Implement or reproduce the smallest TaskFlow slice that demonstrates this ci concept.
Diagnose one representative ci failure using observable evidence instead of trial-and-error.
workshop.why: CI turns repository rules into automated gates. A useful pipeline must be understandable, reproducible locally, secure, and able to fail for the right reasons.
steps: Restate the goal of “Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge” as one observable behavior. Write the success signal before touching code.
Trace the boundary map: git event → runner → install → quality gates → artifact/deploy decision. Mark the one boundary this lesson changes.
Inspect the current repository state and record the exact files, route, table, or runtime involved. Avoid creating an abstraction before you can name the existing owner.
Implement the smallest vertical slice. Add one coherent change, run the narrowest verification command, and read the output before continuing.

Connect the slice to TaskFlow’s phase artifact: .github/workflows/ci.yml plus release/deploy workflows that build once, tag by commit SHA, and gate promotion.. Verify behavior from the outside as a user or API client would.
Create one controlled failure that is safe to reproduce. Predict the symptom first, capture evidence, locate the earliest broken boundary, then fix only that cause.
Close the reference and rebuild or explain the core change from memory. Record what you would monitor or test before trusting the same change in production.

example.caption: Build the quality gate one step at a time
example.code:
name: CI
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: corepack enable
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck && pnpm test && pnpm build

verify: Run the narrowest relevant command or request and require a clean exit/status.
Inspect the boundary-specific evidence: terminal output, Network panel, database row/query plan, test report, container health, or deployment logs.
Repeat the behavior once after the change so a one-off cached or stale result cannot masquerade as success.
breakIt: Rebuilding different artifacts in each environment
Change one assumption in the ci example—identity, input, configuration, ordering, connectivity, or state—and predict the exact symptom before running it.

troubleshooting.investigation: Compare Node/pnpm versions, lockfile state, environment variables, OS assumptions, and generated artifacts.
Set least-privilege permissions at workflow/job level and isolate untrusted pull-request code from secrets.

workshop.challenge: Without copying the final source, create a second small scenario that applies “Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge” to a different TaskFlow resource or input. Write the acceptance criteria first, implement it, and provide the evidence that each criterion is satisfied.
review: What problem does Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge solve in TaskFlow, and what would be observably wrong without it?
Which part of the ci boundary owns the decision, and which neighboring layer must not own it?
What evidence proves the happy path instead of merely suggesting it worked?
Name one realistic failure or abuse case and the first place you would inspect.
If requirements doubled tomorrow, which part of this design should stay stable and which part is allowed to change?

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 33 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 33: CI/CD with GitHub Actions. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
.github/workflows/ci.yml plus release/deploy workflows that build once, tag by commit SHA, and gate promotion.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Build a trustworthy GitHub Actions pipeline that verifies pull requests, creates immutable release artifacts, uses least privilege, caches safely, and controls deployment concurrency.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.
workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.
steps: Create CI triggered by pull_request with read-only contents permission and explicit concurrency cancellation.
Set up Node and pnpm, then install with --frozen-lockfile so manifests cannot drift from the lockfile.
Run lint/typecheck/tests/build as separate clear steps or jobs with understandable failure ownership.
Add dependency/package cache only after correctness works; key it from lockfile inputs.
Create trusted-main release workflow that tags an image/artifact with the commit SHA rather than latest only.
Add environment protection/permissions for deployment and ensure stale production runs are not silently canceled mid-release.
Run the phase mastery checklist without looking at the provided implementation.
Perform a short architecture review and document one trade-off you consciously accepted.

example.caption: Capstone evidence packet
example.code: Requirement -> implementation diff -> verification -> controlled failure -> diagnosis -> final proof

verify: Can read/write a GitHub Actions workflow
Can explain trigger trust boundaries
Can enforce deterministic install
Can build once/promote same artifact
breakIt: Using pull_request_target with untrusted checkout/secrets
Broad write permissions for all jobs

troubleshooting.symptom: You can only continue by copying the reference
troubleshooting.investigation: Return to the mental model and acceptance criteria. Rebuild one smaller slice from first principles before reopening the source.

troubleshooting.symptom: Everything seems to work but proof is weak
troubleshooting.investigation: Choose an external observer: HTTP client, browser, database query, test runner, health endpoint, or deployment log, and capture deterministic evidence.

workshop.challenge: Extend the phase artifact with one requirement not used in the guided example while preserving the same ownership rules and verification strategy.
review: What did you build without a transcript?
Which boundary caused the most reasoning effort?
Which failure gave the strongest evidence?
What shortcut did you deliberately avoid?
What would you automate before repeating this in a team?

# TaskFlow CI/CD Architecture

Pull request -> CI + integration tests -> merge protection -> main -> build immutable web/api images -> GHCR -> protected environment -> Phase 34 deployment.

Rules:
1. CI proves source.
2. Release builds one immutable artifact per commit.
3. Deployment promotes an already-built artifact; it does not rebuild source.
4. Production environment may require approval and exposes secrets only after protection rules pass.
5. Prefer OIDC to long-lived cloud credentials.
6. `GITHUB_TOKEN` gets only the permissions required by each workflow/job.

# TaskFlow GitHub Actions Snapshot

This snapshot is educational and intentionally stops before actual cloud deployment. Phase 33 produces tested, immutable container candidates. Phase 34 connects those candidates to the selected hosting platform.

Workflow examples use current major action tags for readability. GitHub's security guidance recommends full-length commit SHA pinning for immutable third-party action references in hardened production repositories.

# Sources used for Phase 33

- GitHub Docs: PostgreSQL service containers
- GitHub Docs: Secure use reference
- GitHub Docs: workflow syntax and GITHUB_TOKEN permissions
- GitHub Docs: OpenID Connect reference
- GitHub Docs: deployments, environments, concurrency
- Official action release pages for checkout, setup-node, upload-artifact
- Official Docker action release pages for setup-buildx, login, metadata, build-push
- pnpm/action-setup official releases

# Phase 33 verified action lines (2026-09-18)

- actions/checkout: v7 line (latest observed v7.0.1)
- actions/setup-node: v7 line (latest observed v7.0.0)
- pnpm/action-setup: v6 line (latest observed v6.0.9)
- actions/upload-artifact: v7 line (latest observed v7.0.1)
- docker/setup-buildx-action: v4 line (latest observed v4.3.0)
- docker/login-action: v4 line (latest observed v4.6.0)
- docker/metadata-action: v6 line (latest observed v6.2.0)
- docker/build-push-action: v7 line (latest observed v7.2.0)

For production hardening, pin third-party actions to verified full commit SHAs and let Dependabot maintain them. The workflow examples use major tags for readability.

# Phase 33 verification matrix

- PR lint failure blocks CI.
- Type error blocks CI.
- Unit test failure blocks CI.
- PostgreSQL integration test uses committed migrations.
- Missing migration causes integration failure rather than schema drift.
- Docker build succeeds for web and API.
- Release image is tagged with full commit SHA.
- Release workflow has `packages: write` but CI does not.
- Production deployment concurrency prevents overlapping releases.
- Production environment can require approval before secrets are exposed.
- Workflow action dependencies are reviewed/pinned for production.
- Secrets are never echoed.
- Fork PRs do not receive production secrets.
- OIDC-based cloud auth is preferred over static cloud access keys.

Trust client-provided identity because the browser already logged in.
